content_voiceover: This graph tracks the hemoglobin switch across development, with the site of erythropoiesis and the globin chains made shifting together. Erythropoiesis moves from yolk sac, to fetal liver and spleen, to bone marrow by around thirty weeks gestation. Embryonic hemoglobins — Hb Portland, zeta-2-gamma-2, Gower 1, zeta-2-epsilon-2, and Gower 2, alpha-2-epsilon-2 — appear only in the first trimester, with zeta and epsilon production essentially silenced by about ten weeks. HbF, alpha-2-gamma-2, then dominates throughout gestation, and the gamma-to-beta switch to adult hemoglobin is largely complete by about twenty-four weeks after birth. Know the normal adult values: HbA around ninety-seven percent, HbA2 under three percent, HbF under two percent — higher than that should raise suspicion for a hemoglobinopathy. Two other named hemoglobins are testable: HbH, a tetramer of four beta chains, forms when alpha-globin is severely deficient, as in HbH disease; and Hb Bart's, four gamma chains, forms in the most severe alpha-thalassemia, hydrops fetalis, when no functional alpha genes remain. Both bind oxygen too tightly to deliver it to tissue.
keypoints: Erythropoiesis: yolk sac → liver/spleen → bone marrow (~30wk)
Embryonic Hb (Portland, Gower1/2) silenced by ~10 weeks
HbF dominates in utero; switch to HbA ~complete by 24wk postnatal
HbH (β4) and Hb Bart's (γ4) = excess-chain tetramers in α-thalassemia
keypoint_voiceover: Key points on the hemoglobin switch. Erythropoiesis moves from yolk sac, to liver and spleen, to bone marrow by about thirty weeks gestation. Embryonic hemoglobins like Portland and the Gowers disappear by around ten weeks. HbF dominates before birth, and the switch to adult HbA is largely complete by twenty-four weeks after birth. Normal adult values: roughly ninety-seven percent HbA, under three percent HbA2, under two percent HbF. HbH and Hb Bart's are excess-chain tetramers in severe alpha-thalassemia that bind oxygen too tightly to release it.
